name: Gerlos
kurzbeschreibung: Popular holiday destination in the Gerlostal with the Zillertaler Arena and the reservoir Speicher Durlaßboden.
beschreibung:
Overview

Gerlos is located at 1,246 metres above sea level in the picturesque Gerlostal, a sunny side valley branching off the Zillertal in the Tyrolean district of Schwaz, directly on the provincial border with Salzburg. Framed by the rolling alpine meadows of the Kitzbühel Alps to the north and the rugged summits of the Zillertal Alps to the south, the municipality has a population of around 800. The village is known as a snow-sure and vibrant outdoor hotspot combining first-rate winter sports with untouched mountain scenery. Around Gerlos, the terrain broadens into a sunny high-altitude plateau from which five pristine tributary valleys, including the Schönachtal, Krummbachtal, and Schwarzachtal, lead deep into the alpine wilderness. Just a few kilometres up the valley, the turquoise waters of the Durlassboden reservoir form a scenic haven for watersports and summer relaxation.

History

The historical prominence of Gerlos stems from its strategic position along an ancient alpine pass route connecting Tyrol and Salzburg. The name derives from Celtic roots meaning a pointed plot of land and a torrent riverbed; the mountain crossing was first documented in 1154 as saltus gerlaise. From the High Middle Ages until the early 19th century, the Gerlostal fell under the territorial rule of the Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg. Pack animals transported livestock, salt, and South Tyrolean wine across the pass for generations. In 1630, Salzburg Archbishop Paris Lodron upgraded the historic trail into a roadway to transport gold ore mined at nearby Hainzenberg directly to Salzburg without paying foreign tolls. Following the Congress of Vienna in 1816, the crest of the Gerlos Pass became the official provincial border between Tyrol and Salzburg. The parish church of St. Leonhard and Lambert was completed in Baroque style in 1735, crowned with a distinctive onion dome. In 1962, master road engineer Franz Wallack completed the modern Gerlos Alpine Road.

Getting There

By car, visitors travel via the Inntal Autobahn A12 to the Wiesing/Zillertal exit, following the Zillertalstraße B169 to Zell am Ziller. From there, the Gerlosstraße B165 winds uphill for roughly 17 kilometres to Gerlos. From Salzburg and eastern Austria, access is via Mittersill, Krimml, and the scenic Gerlos Alpine Road across the 1,531-metre Gerlos Pass, which is kept open year-round. Rail passengers arrive at Jenbach station aboard ÖBB long-distance services and transfer to the Zillertalbahn to Zell am Ziller. From the station square, regional VVT bus line 4094 operates frequent scheduled services straight into the village centre and to the mountain railway base stations.

Tips

In winter, Gerlos acts as the beating heart of the Zillertal Arena, the largest contiguous ski area in the valley, offering 150 kilometres of groomed pistes and 52 modern lifts extending to 2,500 metres altitude, linking Gerlos to Zell am Ziller, Königsleiten, and Krimml. Freestylers head to the Action Park Kreuzwiese, while the Isskogelbahn gondola provides direct ski access right from the edge of the village. During summer, the scenic Durlassboden reservoir at 1,405 metres features Austria's highest sailing and windsurfing school, boat rentals, and a gentle 10-kilometre lakeside hiking loop with traditional alpine inns. Walkers enjoy car-free side valleys such as the Schönachtal, leading toward the Schönachkees glacier, or stroll to the rustic Krummbachrast alpine hut. An excursion across the pass to the colossal Krimml Waterfalls makes for an unforgettable day out.
